steps.body: Benchmark estimation rounds each fraction to 0, 1/2 or 1 before any renaming happens. 7/8 + 1/12 is about 1 + 0.
steps.narration: Benchmark estimation rounds each fraction to 0, 1/2 or 1 before any renaming happens. 7/8 + 1/12 is about 1 + 0.

widget.prompt: 7/8 + 1/12 — slide to estimate the total in wholes.
widget.lowFeedback: Too low — 7/8 alone is nearly a whole one.
widget.highFeedback: Too high — both fractions are under one whole, so the sum cannot reach two.
widget.successFeedback: About 1 — 7/8 rounds to 1 and 1/12 rounds to 0, and the exact total is 23/24.

predict.reveal: Nearly one plus nearly nothing lands just under one whole.

cml.actionGoal: Rename both fractions to the same piece size, then count the pieces for g5u benchmark.
invariants: Fractions add and subtract only when their pieces are the same size: renaming scales both parts of a fraction and leaves its value untouched, which is what makes g5u benchmark a counting problem once the denominators agree.
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators across, scaling only one part of a fraction when renaming, or forgetting to trade a whole when the top fraction is too small to subtract from.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If only the numerators were made equal instead of the denominators, what would go wrong?

widget.prompt: Estimating 7/8 + 1/12 with benchmarks, which is closest?

options.label: About 1, since 7/8 is nearly 1 and 1/12 is nearly 0
options.feedback: Correct — rounding each fraction to 0, 1/2 or 1 gives a fast and dependable neighbourhood.

options.label: About 2, since both are fractions
options.feedback: Both are under one whole, so their sum cannot approach two.

options.label: About 1/2
options.feedback: 7/8 alone already passes a half, so the total must sit well above it.

options.label: About 8/20, by adding tops and bottoms
options.feedback: Adding across is not addition of fractions, and 8/20 is smaller than 7/8 alone.

widget.prompt: Order 11/12, 3/12, and 10/12 from least to greatest. Which one is in the MIDDLE?

options.feedback: Correct — the pieces are identical twelfths, so ordering the counts orders the fractions.
11/12 holds the MOST of these identical pieces, so it is the greatest, not the middle.
3/12 holds the FEWEST of these identical pieces, so it is the least, not the middle.

widget.prompt: Once renamed, a jug holds 3/6 litre and then 2/6 litre more. Express the total as ?/6. What is the numerator?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 names the piece size; once the pieces match, only the COUNT of them changes.
That count of pieces does not follow once both fractions wear the same denominator.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Give both fractions the same piece size first; after that the pieces simply count.
